summary: ADR-062's organizer-scoped join is code-correct but test-unproven (two vacuous tenant tests)
description:
Found while shaping TKT-260; recorded rather than absorbed, since TKT-260's subject is
`LoadExchangeSwitch` and this is about two tests that already exist elsewhere.

ADR-062's ai-review finding F3 added `AND res.organizer_id = c.organizer_id` to the reservations
join in both reversal claim queries:

- `services/commerce/internal/store/refund_reversal.go:120`
- `services/commerce/internal/store/exchange_reversal.go:122`

The fix is correct. **The tests that appear to cover it cannot fail**, in exactly the shape
AGENTS.md describes:

- `exchange_reversal_smoke_test.go:485` `TestTheClaimedHoldBelongsToTheClaimingTenant`
- `refund_reversal_smoke_test.go:99` `TestClaimedReversalCarriesTheReservationsOrganizerAndHold`

Each seeds **one** tenant, then asserts the returned `hold_id` equals the hold it just seeded. With
a single tenant there is no wrong row to return, so **deleting the organizer predicate from either
production query leaves both tests green.** They name the right case, they are well-commented, and
they observe nothing. `TestTheClaimedHoldBelongsToTheClaimingTenant`'s own comment states the rule
it fails to test: *"an unscoped join is how a row acquires another tenant's hold"*.

**The reachable failing state.** Both joins are FK-to-PK and therefore single-valued, so the
predicate cannot exclude a wrong row — it can only turn a mismatched row into zero rows. Nothing in
the schema constrains `order_refunds.organizer_id` / `order_exchanges.organizer_id` to equal
`reservations.organizer_id` (no cross-table CHECK, no composite FK), so the mismatch is
constructible by direct insert. That is the fixture: seed a claimable row whose `organizer_id`
disagrees with its reservation's, and assert it is **not claimed**.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] Each of the two tests either gains a mismatched-tenant case or is joined by one that asserts
      the row is not claimed.
- [ ] Demonstrate the gap: one run where the new assertions go red with the predicate deleted, and
      the pre-existing assertions stay green. Without that run, "we covered the gap" is
      unfalsifiable (AGENTS.md).
- [ ] The mutation that counts is one **only** the new case can catch — deleting
      `AND res.organizer_id = c.organizer_id`, nothing lower.

Severity: defence-in-depth, same as TKT-260 — no live leak, and per ADR-021 this is honest-writer
consistency, not tamper-evidence. The value is that the predicate stops being unprotected against
a future refactor that "simplifies" the join.

Quality gates: `make check` green; no production code change expected (tests only) — if a test
surfaces a production defect, report it rather than fixing it here.

comments.body:
<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### Filed from TKT-260 shaping — not yet shaped

Needs the 8-item DoR before Gate 1. Likely `risk:low` once shaped (tests only, two files), but that
call belongs to shaping.

The analysis above is done and verified against the schema at `afa333f4` — the shaper should confirm
it still holds rather than re-derive it. The one thing worth re-checking: whether the seed helpers
(`completedRefund`, `settledExchange`) can express a tenant mismatch without tripping `0010`'s
all-or-nothing CHECK constraints, or whether the fixture needs its own insert.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### Shaping verdict: **NOT READY** — 5 met, 3 open (all `owner: human`), and the premise moved

The defect is real and still open. **But TKT-267 changed what a fix can look like, and the ticket's
acceptance criteria are now provably unsatisfiable.** That is a scope decision, not something
shaping should quietly resolve.

#### What I verified by execution, not reading

Deleting `AND res.organizer_id = c.organizer_id` from the final join of **both** claim queries and
running the suite: **all five relevant tests stay green** — the two the ticket names as vacuous, and
TKT-267's two new cross-tenant tests, and the lock-scope test. So the ticket's core claim holds at
HEAD, and TKT-267 did **not** accidentally close it.

#### Why the prescribed fixture can no longer work

TKT-267 added **conjunct 6**: a correlated `EXISTS` in the `claimable` CTE that checks *the same
condition* as the final join, one stage earlier. All three CTEs run in **one statement under one
snapshot**, so the final join only ever sees rows `claimable` already admitted. A mismatched row is
filtered before it gets there.

The ticket says: *"seed a claimable row whose `organizer_id` disagrees with its reservation's, and
assert it is not claimed."* That fixture now goes red for the **wrong reason** — conjunct 6 refuses
it — and would stay green with the final-join predicate deleted. It is the vacuous shape the ticket
was written to eliminate, reintroduced one layer up. **No black-box test can reach that join.**

I also checked the ticket's implicit suggestion of copying TKT-260's
`TestLoadExchangeSwitchRefusesAnExchangeWhoseReservationIsAnotherTenants`. It does **not** transfer:
that test works precisely because `LoadExchangeSwitch` is a single-stage read with nothing upstream
of its join.

#### ⛔ The decision — three options, none obviously right

**Option 1 — retarget, and say so honestly.** Accept that the final join is now unreachable-by-input
and that this is *good*: the property "a mismatched row is never claimed" is fully covered by
conjunct 6's tests. Rewrite the two vacuous tests to assert what they can actually observe, and
replace the deleted-predicate mutation with a comment recording that the final join is defence in
depth whose only remaining value is surviving a refactor that removes conjunct 6. **Cheapest, honest,
and leaves a predicate no test protects.**

**Option 2 — test the fragment, not the query.** Extract the final `SELECT` and exercise it directly
against seeded `claimed`-shaped input. This *can* reach the join. But it tests a string this codebase
otherwise only runs as part of a whole statement — and TKT-267's plan-review explicitly **rejected**
SQL-constant extraction as "how a test starts pinning the harness instead of the contract". Choosing
it now means overruling that, deliberately.

**Option 3 — make the two predicates non-redundant.** If TKT-268 lands option (b) (a denormalized
`source_organizer_id`), conjunct 6 could key on the denormalized column while the final join keeps
checking the real one — they would then disagree on a corrupt row, and the join becomes reachable and
meaningfully testable. **Best outcome, most work, and depends on TKT-268's shape.** This is why
TKT-268 should be planned first.

**My recommendation: option 1, unless TKT-268 chooses (b), in which case option 3.** Option 2 buys
coverage by breaking a rule this codebase adopted for good reasons.

#### Also worth the owner's attention

The ticket's severity line ("no live leak, defence-in-depth") is **still accurate**, and after TKT-267
it is *more* so — the live liveness defect that shared this root cause is now closed. The honest
framing is that this ticket protects a **redundant** predicate against a future refactor. That is a
real but modest value, and it is worth deciding whether it justifies more than option 1.

⛔ **Held at Gate 1** with `scope`, `approach` and `success` open and owned by the human. This is the
DoR working as intended: a ticket whose stated AC cannot be met should not reach Planning, because an
LLM planner will produce a confident plan for an impossible test.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### Gate 1 taken by the owner — option 1 (retarget + record). READY.

All eight DoR items now `met`. The three that were `owner: human` are resolved by the owner's choice
and recorded above; the AC has been **rewritten**, because the original was unsatisfiable and a
ticket that cannot meet its own acceptance must not reach Planning.

**What the owner accepted, stated plainly:** the final join's predicate ends up with no test that can
fail on its deletion. That is the cost of option 1 and it is being taken deliberately, not papered
over — the ticket's deliverable includes a test that *records* the unreachability, so the next reader
finds a stated fact rather than an untested predicate.

**One thing shaping found on re-reading that the original ticket did not have.** It is not just that
`TestTheClaimedHoldBelongsToTheClaimingTenant` seeds one tenant. It derives its expected hold by
running `SELECT r.hold_id ... WHERE o.id=$1 AND r.organizer_id=$2` against the same seed — so the
assertion compares a value **with itself**. That is a strictly worse failure than "one tenant": even
with a second tenant seeded, the test would stay green as long as the expectation is computed that
way. The retarget must fix the *derivation*, not only the fixture. (AGENTS.md — a precondition that
cannot fail.)

**risk:low — claimed.** Tests only, two files, no production code, no auth, no money, no migration,
no CI config. The one carve-out worth naming is that this touches tests guarding a tenancy boundary,
so the work is *about* correctness even though it cannot change behaviour; the plan gate is skipped
but the ai-review pass is not.

<!-- sdlc:stage=ready kind=claim -->
### Claimed — running gateless per `config.gates: autonomous`

**Blockers: zero.** `blocked-by TKT-267` is satisfied — TKT-267 is Done, merged as `bb7cdf35`.
Branch `TKT-266-retarget-vacuous-tenant-tests` off `origin/main` at that commit, so conjunct 6 is
present in the tree this work is written against. That matters: the whole point of the re-scope is
that conjunct 6 exists.

**Selection reason:** taken by name, and it is the natural successor — TKT-267 is what invalidated
this ticket's original plan, so closing it now keeps the two consistent while the context is fresh.

**Risk verdict: `risk:low` CLAIMED — stated explicitly rather than left silent.** All four carve-outs
checked: no auth surface, no money path, no data migration, no CI/deploy config. Two test files, no
production code at all. Under five files.

The one thing that gives me pause, named here so it is in the thread rather than only in my head:
these tests guard a **tenancy boundary**, so the work is *about* a security-adjacent property even
though it cannot change behaviour. I am claiming `risk:low` anyway because the label governs whether
a human approves the *plan*, and there is no design decision left to approve — the owner already
made the only real one at Gate 1 (option 1 over options 2 and 3), and the approach is recorded in the
DoR. The adversarial ai-review pass still runs; `risk:low` skips the plan gate, not the review.

**If the work turns out to need a production change, the label comes off and I say so** — per the
invariant, and per this ticket's own AC 5, which says a test surfacing a production defect gets
*reported*, not fixed here.

Plan gate skipped (`risk:low`) → straight to Building.

<!-- sdlc:stage=coding kind=summary -->
### Coding complete — `main-agent` (`config.models.implement`), PR #312 @ `995456ab`

**Gate** `make check` — sentinel `EXIT=0`, no failure matches in the log body; smoke store 21.9s
(vs 0.611s tagged-out), so the tests ran against the real stack. **Diff:** 2 files, +233/−12,
**tests only**.

#### AC 2 first: the gap, demonstrated

Deleted `AND res.organizer_id = c.organizer_id` from both claim queries and ran the two tests:
**both passed.** That is the run the ticket demands, and it is what makes the rest falsifiable.

#### The ticket's diagnosis was half right, and my first two fixes were themselves vacuous

Recording the failed attempts, because each was a plausible fix that a reviewer would have accepted
and each proved nothing.

**The filed cause** was the single-tenant fixture — real, but not the whole defect. The exchange-side
test derived `want` with `SELECT r.hold_id ... WHERE o.id=$1 AND r.organizer_id=$2` — **the claim's
own join predicate spelled out again**. It compared the query's answer against a value obtained by
asking the same question (AGENTS.md, a precondition that cannot fail). A second tenant would not have
fixed that.

**Attempt 1 — second TENANT, assert the returned hold is not theirs.** Passed under mutation.
`orders.reservation_id` is `UNIQUE REFERENCES reservations(id)` and `reservations.id` is the primary
key (migration 0001), so the join is **FK-to-PK and single-valued**: deleting the organizer predicate
cannot select a different reservation, only turn a mismatched row into zero rows. **That assertion
can never fire, under any fixture.** The original ticket said as much ("assert it is not claimed") and
I had to rediscover it by running the mutation.

**Attempt 2 — decoy reservation on the SAME organizer**, so a by-organizer join is multi-valued.
Still passed: the join returns **both** rows and `claimExchange` stops at the first match, finds the
correct one and reports success.

**What works — count the rows.** The real harm of a lost `id` correlation is **duplication**: one
obligation emitted once per reservation the organizer owns, so the sweep drives it repeatedly and
returns its capacity that many times. Both tests now scan every returned row and assert exactly one.

#### The shadowing tests hit the same trap

First version asserted the malformed row is absent from the OUTPUT — and stayed **green with conjunct
6 deleted**, because the final join drops it just as effectively. The assertion could not distinguish
which stage refused, so it would have claimed to observe shadowing while observing nothing.

Now it asserts the row was never **LEASED**. The lease is written by `claimed`, which runs after
`claimable` and before the final join, so an untouched lease is reachable only if `claimable` refused
— which is exactly the shadowing relationship.

#### Mutation checks

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| delete final-join predicate (both queries) | original tests green → **the gap** |
| join on `organizer` instead of `res.id` (both) | both retargeted tests **RED**, on the row count |
| delete conjunct 6 (both) | both shadowing tests **RED**, on the lease assertion |

#### AC status

- [x] 1 — expectations no longer re-run the predicate under test; fixture makes the wrong answer
      constructible (a decoy reservation on the same organizer, not a second tenant — see above).
- [x] 2 — the gap demonstrated by a run, above.
- [x] 3 — shadowing pinned, and it **fails if conjunct 6 is deleted**.
- [x] 4 — TKT-267's conjunct 6 tests and the lock-scope test stay green.
- [x] 5 — **no production code change.** `git status` showed only the two test files at every commit.
      No test surfaced a production defect, so nothing to report under this AC.
- [x] 6 — `make check` green.

#### One honest note on residual coverage

The final join's organizer predicate still has **no test that fails on its deletion**, and cannot
have one while conjunct 6 shadows it. That is the accepted cost of the owner's option-1 choice at
Gate 1, not an oversight — and the shadowing tests are what stop it from being silent.

<!-- sdlc:stage=ai-review kind=summary -->
### ai-review — `gpt-5.6-luna` (`config.models.aiReview`). One pass, conclusive, 4/4 findings valid.

Run via the companion's `task` command with a defect-hunting brief rather than
`adversarial-review`, which returned zero bytes on TKT-267. Diff given, plan withheld.

| # | Finding | Verdict | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | The two shadowing tests duplicate TKT-267's conjunct-6 tests | **ACCEPTED** | Deleted |
| F2 | …and can pass without proving `claimable` refused | **ACCEPTED — I had missed this** | Deleted |
| F3 | They claim ≤50 unrelated rows on a shared DB, cleaning up only their own seed | **ACCEPTED** | Deleted |
| F4 | "all three CTEs" — there are two plus a final SELECT | **ACCEPTED** | Removed with them |

**F1 I had already found**, by the same two mutations, before the review returned: deleting
`claimable`'s `EXISTS` fails both pairs; deleting the final-join predicate passes both. No mutation
the shadowing tests catch that conjunct 6's do not.

**F2 I had not**, and it is the sharper half. Those tests called an unscoped `limit=50` claim with no
`NextAttemptAt` and no positive control, so with 50 eligible rows ahead of it the malformed row is
unleased and absent *whatever the predicate does*. The reviewer's decisive sentence: *"a claim
implementation that updates no rows would also satisfy the assertions."* That is the harness-pinning
shape — every assertion satisfiable by breaking the instrumentation instead of the logic — in a
ticket whose entire subject is tests that cannot fail. I wrote it while fixing the thing it is an
instance of.

#### Why deleted rather than fixed

Patching F2 means `limit=1`, an oldest malformed row, and a valid control row. At that point they are
line-for-line `TestConjunct6...IsNotLeased` and `TestARefund...IsNotLeased`, which already exist and
already pass. The only thing they would still carry is a failure message explaining shadowing — prose,
which belongs in comments and ADRs, not in a duplicate test. Shipping them would leave decoration
behind in the one ticket that must not.

#### Second pass: NOT run, and why that is the rule rather than a shortcut

The fix diff is **99 deletions and 0 added lines** (`git diff 995456ab..8188b4db` — verified, not
assumed). It introduces no logic, no control flow, no new assertion. The only way a pure deletion
harms is by removing coverage, so that is what I checked rather than argued: after the deletion, the
join-loses-`id`-correlation mutation still turns **both** retargeted tests red, and the full affected
set stays green. One pass, recorded per the rules; the trivia exemption applies.

#### Residual, stated plainly

**The final join's organizer predicate now has no test of any kind** — not even the documentary one I
tried to give it. That was already the accepted cost of the owner's option-1 decision at Gate 1; the
review established that my mitigation was not a mitigation. It is recorded here, in the commit
message, and in the PR so it cannot be mistaken for an oversight later.

The retargeted tests — the ticket's actual deliverable — were found sound: *"the decoy is unreachable
through the correct ID join but reachable under the intended organizer-only mutation. The distinct-hold
guards check the relevant distinction, and cleanup ordering is safe because t.Cleanup runs LIFO."*

<!-- sdlc:stage=po-review kind=summary -->
### Merged as `859c66de`. Self-validated against the REWRITTEN COS.

PR #312 squash-merged, branch deleted. **Verified on `origin/main` itself**, not from the badge:
retargeted tests present, shadowing tests absent, and `git diff bb7cdf35..origin/main` over both
production query files returns **empty** — AC 5 held.

| # | Condition (as rewritten at Gate 1) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Expectations no longer re-run the predicate under test; fixture makes the wrong answer constructible | The exchange test's expectation is read by reservation id alone. The fixture is a decoy reservation on the **same organizer** — not a second tenant, for the reason in AC 1's note below. |
| 2 | The gap demonstrated by a run | Deleted the final-join predicate from both queries → both original tests **passed**. |
| 3 | A test pins the shadowing, and fails if conjunct 6 is deleted | **NOT DELIVERED — withdrawn on review evidence.** See below. |
| 4 | TKT-267's conjunct 6 tests and the lock-scope test stay green | Green in every run, including post-merge. |
| 5 | No production code change | Zero production diff on `origin/main`. No test surfaced a production defect. |
| 6 | `make check` green | Green on both commits and after the merge. |

#### AC 3 was not delivered, and that is the honest outcome

I built it, the review proved it was worthless, and I deleted it rather than ship it. Two reasons,
both verified by running mutations rather than by argument:

- It caught **nothing** conjunct 6's existing tests do not. Same mutations fail both pairs.
- It could pass without proving anything: unscoped `limit=50`, no oldest-row ordering, no positive
  control — so *"a claim implementation that updates no rows would also satisfy the assertions."*
  A test that pins the harness, written while fixing an instance of exactly that.

Making it sound would have made it a line-for-line copy of `TestConjunct6...IsNotLeased`. So the
ticket closes with AC 3 **withdrawn**, not met — recorded here rather than quietly re-scoped.

#### What the reviewer should look at, and the residual

**The final join's organizer predicate has no test of any kind.** Conjunct 6 filters the malformed
row one stage earlier in the same statement, so nothing seedable reaches that join. This was the
accepted cost of the owner's option-1 choice at Gate 1; what changed is that my attempted mitigation
turned out not to be one. It is stated in the commit, the PR guide, and here.

**Worth revisiting if TKT-268 adopts a denormalized `source_organizer_id`** — the two predicates
would stop being redundant and the join would become genuinely testable.

#### What was actually delivered

Both retargeted tests now catch a mutation nothing in the suite caught before: the join losing its
`res.id = o.reservation_id` correlation, whose real harm is **duplication** — one obligation emitted
once per reservation the organizer owns, so the sweep returns the same capacity repeatedly. Verified
red on that mutation both before and after the deletion commit.

<!-- sdlc:stage=done kind=metrics -->
### Closeout — TKT-266, merged `859c66de`, post-merge `make check` green on `main`

Durations from the `sdlc-state` log. Note the ticket sat in Backlog across two sessions: filed and
shaped 23:40–01:14, then re-shaped and run 10:06–10:41 after TKT-267 invalidated its premise.

| stage | duration |
|---|---|
| Backlog (shaping, incl. re-shape after TKT-267) | 23:40 → 10:06 (~34m of work; wall clock spans the gap) |
| Ready (claim) | 10:06:46 → 10:07:06 (20s) |
| Planning | **skipped** — `risk:low` |
| Building — `agent:coding` | 10:07:06 → 10:22:12 (~15m) |
| Building — `agent:ai-review` (1 pass + 3 gate runs) | 10:22:12 → 10:41:21 (~19m) |
| PO Review | 10:41:21 → closeout (~3m) |

**human-wait total:** `n/a (autonomous)` — except Gate 1, which the owner took explicitly, and the
option-1 scope decision, which was a genuine human call this run stopped for.
**diff:** +134/−12 (2 files), tests only.

#### overrides: — blocking objections overridden

**One entry.** Everything else the review raised was accepted and acted on.

1. **AC 3 abandoned rather than delivered.** The review's F1/F2 said the shadowing tests were
   duplicates *and* could pass vacuously. I did not fix them, and I did not ship them — I deleted
   them, which means the ticket's own acceptance criterion 3 is **unmet**. Reviewer's reason: no
   mutation they catch that conjunct 6's tests do not, and an unscoped `limit=50` with no positive
   control makes them satisfiable by a claim that updates nothing. My reason for overriding the AC
   rather than the finding: the AC was written at Gate 1 on my assumption that a shadowing test
   *could* be made meaningful, and that assumption was wrong. Delivering a sound version means
   duplicating `TestConjunct6...IsNotLeased` exactly. **Residual risk carrier: this ticket, closed
   with the gap open** — the final join's organizer predicate has no test of any kind, and TKT-268
   is where it becomes fixable.

Not overrides, recorded so the distinction is clear: F3 (unscoped write side-effect) and F4 (the
false "three CTEs") were fixed by the same deletion.

#### learnings:

1. **A fixture's shape is decided by the JOIN's cardinality, not by the property's name.** Two
   plausible cross-tenant fixtures were unfalsifiable here for structural reasons: the join is
   FK-to-PK, so deleting a predicate yields zero rows rather than a wrong row, and a multi-valued
   mutation returns the right row *alongside* the wrong one — so a helper that stops at the first
   match reports success. Ask what the mutation *does to the result set* (absent? duplicated?
   substituted?) before choosing what to assert. → **`docs/learnings/`** + one line in **`AGENTS.md`**
   under the existing fixture rules.
2. **A test asserting "X is absent from the output" cannot tell WHICH stage refused.** When two
   predicates check the same condition at different stages, absence is satisfied by either; only an
   observation *between* them (here, the lease) distinguishes. This one I found myself, mid-build,
   and it still was not enough to save the test. → same learnings file, same rule family.
3. **The harness-pinning shape reappears in the very ticket that fixes it.** TKT-266's subject is
   tests that observe nothing, and the tests I added to it were satisfiable by a claim that updated
   no rows. Being aware of a failure mode is not protection against it; a cross-model reviewer is.
   → this is already AGENTS.md's cross-model-review rule; **cite it, do not restate it**.
4. **When an AC turns out to be unsatisfiable, withdraw it in the closeout rather than re-scope it
   silently.** → process, `references/quality-practices.md`.

#### retro:

**(1) What would have made this ticket faster or better?**

The re-shape correctly established that the ticket's *fixture* was wrong, and then I wrote two more
wrong fixtures before finding the right one — each discovered only by running a mutation. What was
missing at shaping was a single question: **"what does the mutation do to the result set?"** The DoR's
`approach` item asks for technical direction; it does not ask for the *observable consequence* of the
defect. *Concrete change:* in `references/shaping.md` § When the approach lands on a guard, add — *"and
state what the guard's failure looks like in the OUTPUT: a missing row, a duplicated row, a wrong
value. The fixture and the assertion follow from that, and naming it at shaping costs one read where
discovering it at build time costs a mutation cycle each time."*

**(2) What should the humans change?**

The `risk:low` label skipped the plan gate, and that was right by the rules — but this ticket then
spent three build cycles on fixture design, which is exactly the kind of thing a plan critique
catches cheaply. `risk:low` currently keys on *blast radius* (auth, money, migrations, file count).
It has no notion of **design uncertainty**, and a tests-only ticket can be zero-blast-radius and still
have a hard, wrong-by-default design. *Concrete change:* in `SKILL.md` § Labels, extend the `risk:low`
invariant — *"`risk:low` is about blast radius, not difficulty. If the ticket's central question is
**how to construct a test that can fail**, or any other design question with a non-obvious answer,
keep the plan gate even when the diff is small and touches nothing dangerous."*

**Offered:** both patches, plus the two still-unapplied from TKT-267's retro, are skill/process edits
that go straight to the default branch with no ticket. Four small edits, one commit. Say the word.

<!-- sdlc:stage=done kind=metrics -->
### Retro items: APPLIED — `f8daadf2` on `main`

Both patched and verified on `origin/main`, alongside TKT-267's two. Internal maintenance, no ticket,
local gate green.

- **(1) shaping** — `references/shaping.md` § guard predicates: state what the guard's failure looks
  like in the **output** — missing row, duplicated row, or substituted value — because the fixture
  and the assertion follow from that and the property's name never tells you which. Carries this
  ticket's three rejected fixtures as the worked example, plus the two-stage corollary that cost the
  shadowing tests: "the bad row is absent" is satisfied by either stage and cannot show which one
  refused.
- **(2) SKILL.md** — § Labels: `risk:low` is about **blast radius, not difficulty**. This ticket was
  tests-only, zero production code, correctly `risk:low` by every carve-out, and still spent three
  build cycles on a wrong-by-default design that a plan critique would have caught for one delegated
  read.

Learning items 1–2 from the `learnings:` section (join cardinality decides the fixture; absence
cannot identify the refusing stage) are now **carried by the shaping patch above**, which is where a
future run will actually meet them. Item 3 (the harness-pinning shape recurring inside the ticket
that fixes it) stays a citation of AGENTS.md's cross-model-review rule rather than a new artifact, as
the closeout said. Item 4 (withdraw an unsatisfiable AC in the closeout rather than re-scope it
silently) is **not** patched — it is a one-off judgement this run already demonstrates in its own
`overrides:`, and `quality-practices.md` would gain a rule for a case that has occurred once.

objective.note: Two well-named tests (TestTheClaimedHoldBelongsToTheClaimingTenant, TestClaimedReversalCarriesTheReservationsOrganizerAndHold) seed ONE tenant and so cannot fail when the organizer predicate is deleted from the reversal claim queries' final joins. Confirmed still true at HEAD by executing the mutation.

scope.note: DECIDED by the owner at Gate 1: option 1 (retarget + record). Rewrite the two vacuous tests to assert what they CAN observe, and record — in a test, not only a comment — that the final join is now defence-in-depth shadowed by conjunct 6. Tests-only. Explicitly OUT: extracting the SQL fragment (option 2, rejected — TKT-267's plan-review rejected SQL-constant extraction and that reasoning stands), any schema change (option 3, belongs to TKT-268), and any weakening of conjunct 6 to make a fixture reachable.

uncertainties.note: The reachability question is settled, not open: all three CTEs execute in one statement under one snapshot, so the final join sees exactly the rows `claimable` admitted, and no input or race can present it a mismatched organizer. Verified by mutation, not by reading. The remaining unknown is a product/effort call, which is why it sits under `scope` with owner:human rather than here.

dependencies.note: Depends on TKT-267 having landed (it is what changes the premise). Link added. No other blockers. TKT-268 is a sibling from the same review but touches the same predicate — whoever plans this should check TKT-268's chosen shape first, because option (b) there (a denormalized source_organizer_id) would make option 3 here nearly free.

approach.note: Two problems, not one. (a) BOTH tests seed a single tenant, so there is no wrong row to return. (b) WORSE, and not in the original ticket: TestTheClaimedHoldBelongsToTheClaimingTenant derives its expected hold with `SELECT r.hold_id ... WHERE o.id=$1 AND r.organizer_id=$2` from the SAME single-tenant seed — it compares a value with itself, the precondition-that-cannot-fail shape (AGENTS.md), so it would stay green even against a query returning a hold from anywhere. Fix: seed a SECOND tenant whose reservation is a plausible wrong answer, derive the expectation independently of the query under test, and assert the returned hold is the claimant's AND is not the other tenant's. Reuse the existing exchangePairSharingAClaim helper's integrity guard idiom (assert the two organizers actually differ). Plus a pinning test that asserts the ADR-021-style fact the ticket must not overclaim: conjunct 6 refuses the malformed row, so the final join is unreachable-by-input — written so it FAILS if a future edit removes conjunct 6 and makes it reachable again.

first_slice.note: Whichever option is chosen is one slice, both queries, tests only (option 3 would touch production SQL and is therefore NOT tests-only — that is part of what makes it a human call).

success.note: AC rewritten (the old one was unsatisfiable): (1) each test seeds >=2 tenants and derives its expectation without re-running the query under test; (2) a mutation that makes the claim return a foreign tenant's hold turns them red — demonstrated, not asserted; (3) a test pins that the final-join predicate is currently unreachable-by-input, and that test fails if conjunct 6 is deleted; (4) TKT-267's conjunct 6 tests and the lock-scope test stay green; (5) NO production code change — if a test surfaces a production defect, report it, do not fix it here; (6) make check green.
